summary: More than half the adult population holds a graduate degree — 55.2%, a concentration that reflects the gravitational pull of Stanford University sitting squarely within city limits, flanked by a dense constellation of venture capital firms, biotech labs, and tech headquarters along Sand Hill Road and Page Mill Road. That intellectual infrastructure means you can switch employers without changing your commute: Stanford, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, VMware, Tesla's former HQ, and dozens of startups all draw from the same few square miles, making this a genuine job center rather than a bedroom community. But the affordability math is stark — median home values exceed $2 million against a median household income of roughly $220,000, yielding a price-to-income ratio above 9:1, which means even at the local median income, purchasing requires substantial existing wealth or dual high earners. The physical setting softens the sticker shock: the city stretches from the flat baylands near the eastern marshes up toward the wooded foothills of the Santa Cruz Mountains, and the Baylands Nature Preserve offers miles of levee trails with unobstructed views across the San Francisco Bay. University Avenue provides a genuine walkable downtown with independent coffee shops, sit-down restaurants, and a twice-weekly farmers' market, giving the city center a college-town rhythm despite the suburb-quiet residential streets a few blocks away. Evenings average around 52°F year-round with 9.3 hours of daily sunshine, producing that classic Peninsula pattern of warm dry afternoons and cool fogless nights most of the year. Palo Alto is essentially a small city whose economy runs on knowledge production, where the gap between what the place earns and what it costs to own reveals just how much of the housing market is shaped by accumulated wealth rather than current paychecks.
